claim: Current cost-effective imaging systems can measure only a subset of spatial scales at once.
source: However, current cost-effective imaging systems can measure only a subset of these scales at once.
evidence: This is stated as a limitation of existing technology in the abstract, establishing the problem the MCAM addresses.

claim: The MCAM is a scalable multi-camera array microscope that enables comprehensive high-resolution recording from multiple spatial scales simultaneously.
source: We have created a scalable multi-camera array microscope (MCAM) that enables comprehensive high-resolution recording from multiple spatial scales simultaneously, ranging from structures that approach the cellular scale to large-group behavioral dynamics.
evidence: This is the main claim about the MCAM's capabilities as stated in the abstract.

claim: The MCAM collects data from up to 96 cameras.
source: By collecting data from up to 96 cameras, we computationally generate gigapixel-scale images and movies with a field of view over hundreds of square centimeters at an optical resolution of 18 µm.
evidence: This is a direct statement about the hardware configuration of the MCAM system.

claim: The MCAM generates gigapixel-scale images and movies with a field of view over hundreds of square centimeters at an optical resolution of 18 µm.
source: By collecting data from up to 96 cameras, we computationally generate gigapixel-scale images and movies with a field of view over hundreds of square centimeters at an optical resolution of 18 µm.
evidence: This is a direct measurement of the system's performance characteristics.

claim: The MCAM allows observation of behavior and fine anatomical features of numerous freely moving model organisms including larval zebrafish, fruit flies, nematodes, carpenter ants, and slime mold.
source: This allows us to observe the behavior and fine anatomical features of numerous freely moving model organisms on multiple spatial scales, including larval zebrafish, fruit flies, nematodes, carpenter ants, and slime mold.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental demonstrations with multiple species throughout the manuscript.

claim: The MCAM architecture allows stereoscopic tracking of the z-position of organisms using the overlapping field of view from adjacent cameras.
source: Further, the MCAM architecture allows stereoscopic tracking of the z-position of organisms using the overlapping field of view from adjacent cameras.
evidence: This capability is demonstrated in Figure 2F-G with zebrafish 3D tracking.

claim: Complex biological systems typically include processes that span many levels of organization across spatial scales that vary by multiple orders of magnitude.
source: Complex biological systems typically include processes that span many levels of organization across spatial scales that vary by multiple orders of magnitude (Churchland and Sejnowski, 1988; Couzin and Krause, 2003).
evidence: This is supported by citations to established literature on biological systems.

claim: Schooling or shoaling in fish involves social interactions between multiple individuals across tens of centimeters, but also includes coordinated eye movements, pectoral fin changes, and attendant fluctuations in neural activity at the micrometer scale.
source: For instance, processes such as schooling (Wright and Krause, 2006) or shoaling (Larsch and Baier, 2018) in fish involve social interactions between multiple individuals across tens of centimeters, but also include coordinated eye movements (Harpaz et al., 2021), pectoral fin changes (Green et al., 2013), and attendant fluctuations in neural activity (Fan et al., 2019) at the micrometer scale.
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to published research on fish behavior.

claim: No single imaging system currently allows for unrestricted access to each spatial scale simultaneously, which requires the ability to jointly observe a very large field of view while maintaining a high spatial resolution.
source: Currently, no single imaging system allows for unrestricted access to each scale simultaneously, which requires the ability to jointly observe a very large field of view (FOV) while maintaining a high spatial resolution.
evidence: This establishes the gap in existing technology that the MCAM addresses.

claim: Imaging systems typically make tradeoffs in their measurement process between FOV and resolution.
source: Hence, imaging systems typically make tradeoffs in their measurement process between FOV and resolution.
evidence: This is a general principle of optical imaging systems.

claim: Many neuronal imaging methods typically require an animal to be head-fixed or tethered.
source: For example, many neuronal imaging methods typically require an animal to be head-fixed or tethered (Ahrens et al., 2013; Harvey and Svoboda, 2007), which restricts the natural behavioral repertoire (Hamel et al., 2015) and inhibits spontaneous movement (Kim et al., 2017; O'Malley et al., 2004).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published research on neuronal imaging methods.

claim: Head-fixation or tethering restricts the natural behavioral repertoire and inhibits spontaneous movement.
source: For example, many neuronal imaging methods typically require an animal to be head-fixed or tethered (Ahrens et al., 2013; Harvey and Svoboda, 2007), which restricts the natural behavioral repertoire (Hamel et al., 2015) and inhibits spontaneous movement (Kim et al., 2017; O'Malley et al., 2004).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published research on the effects of head-fixation.

claim: Closed-loop mechanical tracking microscopes have been developed to address the challenge of imaging freely moving organisms.
source: Closed-loop mechanical tracking microscopes have recently been developed in an attempt to address this challenge and have acquired impressive high-resolution optical measurements of behavior (Johnson et al., 2020; Reiter et al., 2018), and both behavior and fluorescence (Cong et al., 2017; Kim et al., 2017; Nguyen et al., 2017; Susoy et al., 2021; Symvoulidis et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published research on tracking microscopes.

claim: Tracking microscopes are limited to centering the field of view to a single organism.
source: While such tracking strategies have recently revealed dynamics between persistent internal states within the brain during unconstrained behavior, for example. Such tracking strategies are powerful, but the optical apparatus has been limited to centering the field of view to a single organism.
evidence: This is stated as a limitation of existing tracking microscope technology.

claim: Tracking strategies have revealed the dynamics of internal states within the brain during unconstrained behavior.
source: For instance, such tracking strategies have revealed the dynamics of internal states within the brain during unconstrained behavior (Marques et al., 2019), even when an individual is interacting with others (Grover et al., 2020; Susoy et al., 2021).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published research using tracking strategies.

claim: Tracking systems are limited to tracking one animal at any given time and do not effectively scale to the challenge of jointly observing the free movement and spatiotemporally varying interactions of many organisms at high resolution over a large area.
source: Such systems are limited to tracking one animal at any given time, and do not effectively scale to the challenge of jointly observing the free movement and spatiotemporally varying interactions of many organisms at high resolution over a large area.
evidence: This is stated as a limitation of existing tracking systems.

claim: Time-sequential scanning-based imaging approaches are routinely employed to capture image data from larger areas at high-resolution.
source: Alternatively, time-sequential scanning-based imaging approaches are routinely employed to capture image data from larger areas at high-resolution.
evidence: This is a description of existing imaging approaches.

claim: Time sequential measurements can be obtained either by mechanical movement, the use of shifting microlens arrays, or via illumination steering as a function of time.
source: Time sequential measurements can be obtained either by mechanical movement (Potsaid et al., 2005), the use of shifting microlens arrays (Orth and Crozier, 2013; Orth and Crozier, 2012) or via illumination steering as a function of time (Ashraf et al., 2021; Gustafsson, 2005; Mudry et al., 2012; Zheng et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published research on time-sequential imaging methods.

claim: Time-sequential imaging strategies are not able to simultaneously observe living processes at high resolution over a large area.
source: Unfortunately, such time-sequential imaging strategies are not able to simultaneously observe living processes at high resolution over a large area: for instance, the movement of multiple individuals can change position during the slow acquisition cycle, and thus generate ambiguities in the acquired data.
evidence: This is stated as a limitation of time-sequential imaging approaches.

claim: A common strategy to simultaneously observe many freely moving organisms within a large FOV is to reduce imaging system magnification and resolution.
source: To simultaneously observe many freely moving organisms within a medium petri dish, well plate or an alternative arena that occupies a large FOV, a common strategy is to simply reduce imaging system magnification and resolution (i.e. to 'zoom out'; Buchanan et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to published research and describes a common practice.

claim: Reducing magnification and resolution is commonly performed in high-content screening experiments in toxicology and pharmacology.
source: This is commonly performed in high-content screening experiments in toxicology (Mathias et al., 2012) and pharmacology (Bruni et al., 2014; Rihel et al., 2010), for example, where imaging many organisms is critical to discovery.
evidence: This is supported by citations to published research in toxicology and pharmacology.

claim: Reducing magnification and resolution necessarily trades off spatial resolution for joint observation and can miss certain morphological features and behavioral signatures.
source: However, such an approach necessarily must trade off spatial resolution for joint observation and can thus miss certain morphological features and behavioral signatures.
evidence: This is stated as a limitation of the zoom-out approach.

claim: Geometrical optical aberrations increase with the surface area of a lens when its diameter increases.
source: Unfortunately, geometrical optical aberrations increase with the surface area of a lens when its diameter increases (Lohmann, 1989).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to published research on optical aberrations.

claim: The number of corrective lenses required to compensate for aberrations quickly increases in a nonlinear manner as lens diameter increases.
source: The number of corrective lenses required to compensate for these aberrations quickly increases, as does the overall lens system scale, in a nonlinear manner (Lohmann, 1989).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to published research on lens design.

claim: Additional corrective lenses rapidly increase the size, weight, complexity and cost of imaging optics.
source: These additional corrective lenses rapidly increase the size, weight, complexity and cost of imaging optics (Brady et al., 2018; Mait et al., 2018) which generally limits most commercially available microscope lenses to transfer less than 50 megapixels of resolved optical information to the image plane (Zheng et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published research on imaging optics.

claim: Most commercially available microscope lenses transfer less than 50 megapixels of resolved optical information to the image plane.
source: These additional corrective lenses rapidly increase the size, weight, complexity and cost of imaging optics (Brady et al., 2018; Mait et al., 2018) which generally limits most commercially available microscope lenses to transfer less than 50 megapixels of resolved optical information to the image plane (Zheng et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to published research on microscope lens capabilities.

claim: Complex lens systems specifically designed to address the megapixel challenge have not been able to increase resolved optical information beyond several hundred megapixels.
source: Complex lens systems specifically designed to address this challenge have not been able to increase this quantity beyond several hundred megapixels (McConnell et al., 2016; McConnell and Amos, 2018; Sofroniew et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published research on advanced lens systems.

claim: The largest digital image sensors currently available contain at most several hundred megapixels.
source: At the same time, the largest digital image sensors currently available also contain at most several hundred megapixels (Canon, 2022), which suggests a natural limit to single lens imaging systems precluding direct acquisition of gigapixel-scale image data.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Canon's sensor specifications.

claim: A 3.2-gigapixel digital camera for a specialized Large Synoptic Survey Telescope was developed, but its cost of $168 million is prohibitive for most individual labs.
source: Recently, a 3.2-gigapixel digital camera for a specialized Large Synoptic Survey Telescope was developed, but its cost, $168 million, is prohibitive for most individual labs.
evidence: This is a factual statement about an existing gigapixel camera system and its cost.

claim: The MCAM is an inexpensive, scalable system whose cost scales linearly with the number of pixels.
source: To overcome these challenges, and extend observational capabilities to the gigapixel regime, we designed and constructed an inexpensive, scalable Multi Camera Array Microscope (MCAM) (Figure 1A), a system whose cost scales linearly with the number of pixels.
evidence: This is a claim about the cost structure of the MCAM system.

claim: The MCAM design is significantly less expensive than other available large-area, high-resolution imaging systems as it leverages relatively inexpensive components.
source: This design is significantly less expensive than other available large-area, high-resolution imaging systems as it leverages relatively inexpensive components (see Methods).
evidence: This is supported by the cost breakdown provided in the Methods section.

claim: The MCAM collects data in parallel from an arbitrarily sized rectangular grid of closely spaced modern CMOS image sensors.
source: The MCAM collects data in parallel from an arbitrarily sized rectangular grid of closely spaced modern CMOS image sensors (each with ~107 pixels that are 1 µm in size, Appendix 1—figure 1), which are currently produced in large volumes for the cell phone camera market and are thus readily available in many varieties and at low-cost.
evidence: This describes the hardware architecture of the MCAM system.

claim: Each MCAM image sensor is outfitted with its own high-resolution lens to capture image data from a unique sample plane area.
source: Each MCAM image sensor is outfitted with its own high-resolution lens to capture image data from a unique sample plane area (Figure 1A, zoom in).
evidence: This describes the optical configuration of the MCAM system, shown in Figure 1A.

claim: The MCAM sensors and lenses are arranged such that their fields-of-view partially overlap with their immediate neighbors.
source: The MCAM sensors and lenses are arranged such that their fields-of-view partially overlap with their immediate neighbors (Appendix 1—figure 2), which ensures that image data are jointly acquired from a continuous area (Figure 1B).
evidence: This describes the arrangement of sensors and is shown in Appendix 1—figure 2 and Figure 1B.

claim: The parallelized image acquisition geometry can, in theory, be scaled to produce an arbitrarily large FOV.
source: Such a parallelized image acquisition geometry (Brady et al., 2018) can, in theory, be scaled to produce an arbitrarily large FOV.
evidence: This is a theoretical claim about the scalability of the MCAM architecture, supported by a citation.

claim: The MCAM designs with up to 96 cameras allow recording of information-rich bright-field gigapixel videos of multiple freely moving species at 18 μm full-pitch optical resolution over a 384 cm2 FOV.
source: Here, we present MCAM designs with up to 96 cameras that allow us to record information-rich bright-field gigapixel videos of multiple freely moving species, including Carpenter ants (Camponotus spp.), fruit flies (Drosophila melanogaster), nematodes (Caenorhabditis elegans), zebrafish (Danio rerio), and the amoeboid slime mold (Physarum polycephalum) (Nakagaki et al., 2000) at 18 μm full-pitch optical resolution (i.e. the ability to resolve two bars with a center to center spacing of 18 μm) over a 384 cm2 FOV.
evidence: This is a summary of the MCAM's demonstrated capabilities with multiple species.

claim: The MCAM offers a scalable platform that overcomes current imaging bottlenecks and allows simultaneous observation of phenomena spanning from the microscopic to the macroscopic regimes.
source: As a unique approach to address the FOV/resolution tradeoff, the MCAM offers a scalable platform that overcomes current imaging bottlenecks and allows us to simultaneously observe phenomena spanning from the microscopic to the macroscopic regimes.
evidence: This is a summary claim about the MCAM's capabilities and advantages.

claim: The first constructed gigapixel MCAM system consists of 96 individual CMOS sensors, lenses, and associated read-out electronics.
source: Our first constructed gigapixel MCAM system consists of 96 individual complementary metal oxide semiconductor (CMOS) sensors, lenses, and associated read-out electronics that transmit recorded image data from all sensors to computer memory for offline processing.
evidence: This describes the hardware configuration of the MCAM system.

claim: The MCAM sensors and lenses are arranged in an aggregate 8x12 array and composed of 4 individual 24-sensor MCAM imaging units placed in a 2x2 array.
source: The sensors and lenses (i.e. micro-cameras) are arranged in an aggregate 8x12 array and composed of 4 individual 24-sensor MCAM imaging units placed in a 2x2 array, as sketched in Appendix 1—figure 1.
evidence: This describes the physical arrangement of the MCAM system, shown in Appendix 1—figure 1.

claim: Each CMOS sensor contains 10 megapixels (4320x2432) and a pixel size of 1.4 µm for a 6 mm x 3.4 mm active area.
source: Each CMOS sensor (Omnivision, OV10823) contains 10 megapixels (4320x2432) and a pixel size of 1.4 µm for a 6 mm x 3.4 mm active area.
evidence: This provides technical specifications of the CMOS sensors used in the MCAM.

claim: The sensors were placed at a 19 mm pitch.
source: The sensors were placed at a 19 mm pitch, and their rectangular active area allows us to capture overlapping field-of-view information primarily along one dimension for stereo-based depth tracking and dual-channel fluorescence imaging.
evidence: This describes the physical spacing of sensors in the MCAM.

claim: The imaging system's total number of recorded pixels per frame is 0.96 gigapixels.
source: The imaging system's total number of recorded pixels per frame is 0.96 gigapixels.
evidence: This is a direct measurement of the MCAM's pixel count.

claim: The MCAM can operate in a 'full-frame' mode that records video data from all 96 micro-cameras at an aggregate frame rate of approximately 1 frame per second.
source: The MCAM offers two modes of operation. First, it can operate in a 'full-frame' mode that records video data from all 96 micro-cameras at an aggregate frame rate of approximately 1 frame per second (see timing diagram in Appendix 1—figure 4B–C).
evidence: This describes one operational mode of the MCAM system.

claim: The per-frame exposure time for each individual camera can be reduced to approximately 1ms to limit any per-frame motion blur.
source: The per-frame exposure time for each individual camera can be reduced to approximately 1ms to limit any per-frame motion blur.
evidence: This describes a technical capability of the MCAM system.

claim: The MCAM architecture offers the flexibility to read data from a smaller number of sensors at a higher frame rate.
source: The MCAM architecture also offers the flexibility to read data from a smaller number of sensors at a higher frame rate.
evidence: This describes an alternative operational mode of the MCAM system.

claim: A 'single-sensor' mode of operation allows selective recording of video data from up to four electronically assigned micro-cameras at a frame rate of approximately 12 frames per second.
source: For example, a 'single-sensor' mode of operation allows us to selectively record video data from up to four electronically assigned micro-cameras at a frame rate of approximately 12 frames per second (Appendix 1—figure 5).
evidence: This describes another operational mode of the MCAM system.

claim: Each of the 96 cameras utilizes a multi-element 12 mm diameter mount lens with 25 mm focal length and 2.5 f-number.
source: Each of the 96 cameras utilizes a multi-element 12 mm diameter mount lens (Edmund Optics 58–207, 25 mm focal length, 2.5 f-number), with an 18 mm maximum outer diameter that currently sets the MCAM's inter-camera spacing (to 19 mm).
evidence: This provides technical specifications of the lenses used in the MCAM.

claim: The MCAM lenses offer approximately 18 µm full-pitch resolution at a 150 mm working distance that extends across the entire per-sensor image FOV.
source: As shown in Appendix 1—figure 2, these lenses offer approximately 18 µm full-pitch resolution at a 150 mm working distance that extends across the entire per-sensor image FOV with the employed 10 Megapixel rectangular image sensors (1.4 µm pixels, 3.4 mm x 6 mm).
evidence: This is a measurement of the optical resolution of the MCAM system, shown in Appendix 1—figure 2.

claim: The system's theoretical Rayleigh criterion for axial resolution under incoherent imaging conditions is DRay = 0.28 mm.
source: First, we use the system's theoretical Rayleigh criterion for axial resolution under incoherent imaging conditions to estimate DRay = 0.28 mm.
evidence: This is a calculated theoretical value for the MCAM's axial resolution.

claim: The axial sample range across which lateral resolution remains within a factor of 2 of its maximum value at the plane of best focus is DRes = 2.54 mm.
source: Second, we experimentally measured the axial sample range across which lateral resolution remains within a factor of 2 of its maximum value at the plane of best focus as DRes = 2.54 mm, which we found to be a useful measure of practical axial imaging extent.
evidence: This is an experimental measurement of the MCAM's depth of field.

claim: The full-width half-maximum of image contrast as a function of axial distance from the plane of best focus is DCon = 1.95 mm.
source: Third, we experimentally measured the full-width half-maximum of image contrast (defined as the average mean image gradient magnitude of a resolution target) as a function of axial distance from the plane of best focus as DCon = 1.95 mm.
evidence: This is an experimental measurement of the MCAM's depth of field based on image contrast.

claim: The current MCAM design offers approximately 52% image overlap along the longer sensor dimension and <10% overlap along the shorter image dimension.
source: By using rectangular image sensors with a height/width ratio of 1/1.8, the current MCAM design offers approximately 52% image overlap along the longer sensor dimension and <10% overlap along the shorter image dimension.
evidence: This describes the overlapping field-of-view configuration of the MCAM.

claim: The overlapping field-of-view configuration guarantees that any point within the object plane (neglecting edge regions) is imaged by at least two micro-cameras.
source: This overlapping field-of-view configuration is diagrammed in Appendix 1—figures 2 and 4 and guarantees that any point within the object plane (neglecting edge regions) is imaged by at least two micro-cameras.
evidence: This is a consequence of the MCAM's design, shown in Appendix 1—figures 2 and 4.

claim: Packaged 10 MP CMOS sensors were $30 apiece in quantities of 100.
source: Packaged 10 MP CMOS sensors (Omnivision OV10823) were $30 apiece in quantities of 100.
evidence: This is a factual statement about component costs for the MCAM.

claim: Imaging lenses were $75 apiece in quantities of 100.
source: Imaging lenses were $75 apiece in quantities of 100.
evidence: This is a factual statement about component costs for the MCAM.

claim: FPGAs were $267 apiece for 16 units.
source: FPGAs were $267 apiece for 16 units.
evidence: This is a factual statement about component costs for the MCAM.

claim: For the presented MCAM with 96 imagers, the total price of key components is $14,352.
source: For the presented MCAM with 96 imagers, the total price of these key components is $14,352.
evidence: This is a calculated total cost based on the component prices listed.

claim: A continuous recording session at 0.74 Hz lasted almost one hour and resulted in 2.5 TB of unstitched data (2649 frames, 962 MB per frame) and 1.17 TB stitched data (442 MB per image).
source: A continuous recording session at 0.74 Hz lasted almost one hour resulted in 2.5 TB of unstitched data (2649 frames, 962 MB per frame) and 1.17 TB stitched data (442 MB per image).
evidence: This is a measurement of data volume from an actual MCAM recording session.

claim: The system exploits the rapid current read/write speeds for individual solid state drives on a single personal computer (achieving approx. 1 GB/s).
source: The system exploits the rapid current read/write speeds for individual solid state drives on a single personal computer (achieving approx. 1 GB/s), and marks a significant speedup from previously published gigapixel imaging systems (Brady et al., 2012).
evidence: This is a measurement of the MCAM's data transfer speed and comparison to prior work.

claim: In an MCAM image, a zebrafish (8 dpf) is captured by 9699±2758 pixels (n=93 zebrafish).
source: In an MCAM image, a zebrafish (8 dpf) is captured by 9699±2758 pixels (n=93 zebrafish), which is significantly higher than in standard imaging systems.
evidence: This is a measurement of pixel count per zebrafish in MCAM images.

claim: When using a single 20 MP camera with the same large-FOV, fish would be represented by less than 400 pixels.
source: For example, when using a single 20 MP camera with the same large-FOV, fish would be represented by less than 400 pixels, and even less in older juvenile fish (Romero-Ferrero et al., 2019).
evidence: This is a comparison calculation showing the advantage of MCAM over standard cameras.

claim: For a standard 3 MP camera sensor imaging a comparable FOV, a fish occupies less than ~100 pixels.
source: For a standard 3 MP camera sensor imaging a comparable FOV, a fish occupies less than ~100 pixels (Figure 1E).
evidence: This is a comparison calculation shown in Figure 1E.

claim: Stereoscopic depth measurement using the MCAM yields approximately 100 µm accuracy in depth localization over a >5 mm depth range.
source: Using this stereoscopic depth measurement approach yields approximately 100 µm accuracy in depth localization over a>5 mm depth range (see Appendix 1—figure 7 and associated Appendix 1 for experimental support).
evidence: This is a measurement of the MCAM's depth tracking accuracy, with experimental support in Appendix 1—figure 7.

claim: Videos captured approximately 58,000 worms per frame in C. elegans experiments.
source: Videos captured ~58,000 worms per frame, captured at about 450 pixels per worm within a typical gigapixel video (averaged across 20 frames, single frame in Figure 3A–C, top).
evidence: This is a measurement of organism count and pixel resolution in C. elegans experiments.

claim: The NYL2629 C. elegans strain shows previously unreported swarming behavior.
source: Surprisingly, both the unc-3 mutants, and especially the NYL2629 strain show previously unreported swarming behavior.
evidence: This is a novel observation made using the MCAM system.

claim: Approximately 3 days after being transferred to a new nutrient lawn, the NYL2629 strain began to form tight swarms that tiled most of the petri dish in a semi-periodic fashion.
source: Approximately 3 days after being transferred to a new nutrient lawn, the NYL2629 strain began to form tight swarms that tiled most of the petri dish in a semi-periodic fashion (Figure 3B), as has been observed in other strains (de Bono and Bargmann, 1998).
evidence: This is an observation of swarming behavior in the NYL2629 strain, shown in Figure 3B.

claim: The unc-3 mutant C. elegans exhibited large wavefronts of worm aggregates (2–3 cm wide).
source: Based on the hypothesis that this could be driven by partial loss of function in the reporter strain, we then tested for such effects more directly in an unc-3 mutant, where we observed qualitatively different swarming behavior: large wavefronts of worm aggregates (2–3 cm wide) (Figure 3C).
evidence: This is an observation of swarming behavior in the unc-3 mutant, shown in Figure 3C.

claim: Aggregative behavior was not observed in the wildtype C. elegans line.
source: Notably, such aggregative behavior was not observed in the wildtype line (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is a negative observation in the wildtype line, shown in Figure 3A.

claim: Recent research on collective behavior has demonstrated that swarming behaviors are modulated by various factors, including oxygen levels and animal density.
source: Recent research on collective behavior has demonstrated that swarming behaviors are modulated by various factors, including oxygen levels and animal density (Demir et al., 2020; Ding et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published research on C. elegans swarming behavior.

claim: The MCAM is a useful tool for the quantitative study of factors that control social clustering and swarming in C. elegans.
source: While further investigation of the underlying causes and spatiotemporal features of swarming in these different strains is needed, our data clearly demonstrate that the MCAM is a useful tool for the quantitative study of factors that control social clustering and swarming in C. elegans (Figure 3E).
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the C. elegans experiments, with data shown in Figure 3E.

claim: Physarum polycephalum pseudopodia will envelope nutrients in its environment, foraging over a search path spanning many hundreds of square centimeters.
source: For instance, its pseudopodia will envelope nutrients in its environment, foraging over a search path spanning many hundreds of square centimeters (Gawlitta et al., 1980; Rodiek and Hauser, 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published research on slime mold behavior.

claim: The MCAM observed the well-known ability of the slime-mold to traverse mazes, though on much larger spatial scales.
source: Exploiting this, we observed the well-known ability of the slime-mold to traverse mazes, though on much larger spatial scales (Figure 4A; Video 7; Nakagaki et al., 2000).
evidence: This is an observation of slime mold behavior using the MCAM, shown in Figure 4A and Video 7, with citation to prior work.

claim: Using time-lapse imaging with a 24-camera MCAM array, data was acquired over a 46-hr period, showing the cumulative growth and exploration of a standard 10 cm diameter petri dish that had been seeded with oatmeal flakes.
source: Also, using time-lapse imaging with a 24-camera MCAM array (0.24 gigapixels), we acquired data over a 46-hr period, showing the cumulative growth and exploration of a standard 10 cm diameter petri dish that hadbeen seeded with oatmeal flakes (Video 8).
evidence: This describes a time-lapse experiment with slime mold, shown in Video 8.

claim: By switching to single-camera acquisition mode to acquire at a higher frame rate, the well-known cytoplasmic flow within individual plasmodia was observed.
source: Further, by switching to single-camera acquisition mode to acquire at a higher frame rate, we observed the well-known cytoplasmic flow within individual plasmodia (Durham and Ridgway, 1976), involving particulate matter of tens of square microns, flowing across multiple centimeters (Video 9).
evidence: This is an observation of cytoplasmic flow in slime mold, shown in Video 9, with citation to prior work.

claim: Carpenter ants are nocturnal animals, and their activity levels are very tightly locked to ambient light.
source: Carpenter ants are nocturnal animals, and their activity levels are very tightly locked to ambient light (Narendra et al., 2017; Sharma et al., 2004).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published research on Carpenter ant behavior.

claim: When light and dark cycles were alternated with small groups of ants, clear fluctuations in activity levels with light cycles were observed, including the dissolution of tight clusters of 'sleeping ants' with increased movement.
source: When we alternated light and dark cycles with small groups of ants, we observed clear fluctuations in activity levels with light cycles, including the dissolution of tight clusters of 'sleeping ants' with increased movement (Figure 4B), but also social interactions and grooming (pulling on antennae with legs; Video 10).
evidence: This is an observation of Carpenter ant behavior using the MCAM, shown in Figure 4B and Video 10.

claim: The MCAM allowed observation of large-scale social behavioral patterns in adult fruit flies, such as face-to-face interactions, and mutations in the wings such as curling.
source: The MCAM allowed us to observe large-scale social behavioral patterns in adult fruit flies, such as face-to-face interactions, and mutations in the wings such as curling (Figure 4C, Video 11).
evidence: This is an observation of Drosophila behavior using the MCAM, shown in Figure 4C and Video 11.

claim: Small features of individual flies could be seen, such as hairs on individual legs, grooming behavior, and the sex of each animal.
source: At the same time, we could see small features of individual flies, such as hairs on individual legs, grooming behavior, and the sex of each animal (Figure 4C, inset).
evidence: This demonstrates the resolution capabilities of the MCAM for Drosophila imaging, shown in Figure 4C inset.

claim: The MCAM technology enables a new suite of imaging experiments for fluorescent specimens, such as tracking freely moving organisms that emit fluorescence via neuronal genetically encoded calcium indicators.
source: Finally, the MCAM technology also enables a new suite of imaging experiments for fluorescent specimens, such as tracking freely moving organisms that emit fluorescence via neuronal genetically encoded calcium indicators, such as GCaMP6 (Dana et al., 2016).
evidence: This is a claim about the MCAM's fluorescence imaging capabilities, with citation to GCaMP6.

claim: After outfitting the MCAM imaging system for epi-fluorescence imaging, wide-field fluorescence video of multiple freely moving Drosophila larvae and freely swimming zebrafish was captured.
source: After outfitting the MCAM imaging system for epi-fluorescence imaging, we captured wide-field fluorescence video of multiple freely moving Drosophila larvae and freely swimming zebrafish.
evidence: This describes fluorescence imaging experiments performed with the MCAM.

claim: The MCAM's overlapping fields-of-view were utilized to jointly capture two fluorescence spectral channels simultaneously (i.e. both red and green fluorescence emission) within its recorded videos.
source: We also utilized the MCAM's overlapping fields-of-view to jointly capture two fluorescence spectral channels simultaneously (i.e. both red and green fluorescence emission) within its recorded videos, which may be applied to ratiometric fluorescent image analysis in future studies.
evidence: This describes a dual-channel fluorescence imaging capability of the MCAM.

claim: The MCAM's parallelized imaging design overcomes the limitations of single-objective and single-sensor systems, allowing the acquisition of high-resolution images over a large, in principle infinite FOV.
source: Our parallelized imaging design overcomes the limitations of single-objective and single-sensor systems, allowing the acquisition of high-resolution images over a large, in principle infinite FOV.
evidence: This is a summary claim about the advantages of the MCAM's design.

claim: Prior designs have considered multiple microscopes to image distinct regions in parallel, or via cascaded multiscale lens designs that can yield light-field-type imaging measurements.
source: While prior designs have considered multiple microscopes to image distinct regions in parallel (Weinstein et al., 2004), or via cascaded multiscale lens designs (Fan et al., 2019) that can yield light-field-type imaging measurements (Broxton et al., 2013; Levoy et al., 2009), the MCAM provides a novel, flexible arrangement that can monitor phenomena in freely moving organisms at multiple spatial scales.
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work on multi-microscope and multiscale lens designs.

claim: The MCAM provides a novel, flexible arrangement that can monitor phenomena in freely moving organisms at multiple spatial scales.
source: While prior designs have considered multiple microscopes to image distinct regions in parallel (Weinstein et al., 2004), or via cascaded multiscale lens designs (Fan et al., 2019) that can yield light-field-type imaging measurements (Broxton et al., 2013; Levoy et al., 2009), the MCAM provides a novel, flexible arrangement that can monitor phenomena in freely moving organisms at multiple spatial scales.
evidence: This is a claim about the novelty and advantages of the MCAM compared to prior work.

claim: The number of cameras can be varied to produce different FOVs with varying frame rates, depending on the targeted imaging application.
source: The number of cameras can be varied to produce different FOVs with varying frame rates, depending on the targeted imaging application.
evidence: This describes the flexibility of the MCAM design.

claim: The working distance can be changed to jointly increase or decrease the degree of inter-camera FOV overlap to unlock novel functionality.
source: The working distance can also be changed to jointly increase or decrease the degree of inter-camera FOV overlap to unlock novel functionality.
evidence: This describes another aspect of the MCAM's design flexibility.

claim: By adopting a parallelized approach to video acquisition, the MCAM removes a longstanding bottleneck of current single-camera microscope designs to provide researchers with greater flexibility.
source: By adopting a parallelized approach to video acquisition, the MCAM removes a longstanding bottleneck of current single-camera microscope designs to provide researchers with greater flexibility, in particular for observing model organisms at high-resolution in an unconstrained manner.
evidence: This is a summary claim about the advantages of the MCAM's parallelized design.

claim: The MCAM demonstrated two unique capabilities: 3D tracking and simultaneous acquisition of fluorescence images from two unique spectral bands.
source: We have also demonstrated two unique capabilities of the MCAM's multi-lens architecture – 3D tracking and simultaneous acquisition of fluorescence images from two unique spectral bands (see example in Appendix 1—figure 8).
evidence: This is a summary of two novel capabilities demonstrated with the MCAM, with example in Appendix 1—figure 8.

claim: 3D tracking opens up a new dimension to behavioral analysis.
source: The former functionality opens up a new dimension to behavioral analysis, while the latter could lead to novel fluorescence imaging experiments with additional development and refinement.
evidence: This is a claim about the potential impact of the MCAM's 3D tracking capability.

claim: Dual-channel fluorescence imaging could lead to novel fluorescence imaging experiments with additional development and refinement.
source: The former functionality opens up a new dimension to behavioral analysis, while the latter could lead to novel fluorescence imaging experiments with additional development and refinement.
evidence: This is a speculative claim about the potential of the MCAM's dual-channel fluorescence capability.

claim: There are likely a wide variety of alternative exciting functionalities that MCAM overlapped sampling can facilitate, such as dense height map estimation at high resolution over large areas via photogrammetric methods.
source: There are likely a wide variety of alternative exciting functionalities that MCAM overlapped sampling can facilitate, such as dense height map estimation at high resolution over large areas via photogrammetric methods (Zhou et al., 2021).
evidence: This is a speculative claim about potential future applications of the MCAM, with citation to photogrammetric methods.

claim: The MCAM was only able to sample gigapixel images at 1 Hz for up to 60 min.
source: First, while we were only able to sample gigapixel images at 1 Hz for up to 60 min – a significant increase in speed and duration from previous published efforts (Brady et al., 2012) – many biological applications could benefit from much faster acquisition rates.
evidence: This is a stated limitation of the current MCAM system, with comparison to prior work.

claim: The current acquisition speed of 1 Hz is too slow to determine specific patterns in swim kinematics in freely swimming zebrafish.
source: For instance, our current acquisition speed of 1 Hz is too slow to determine specific patterns in swim kinematics in freely swimming zebrafish (Marques et al., 2018).
evidence: This is a stated limitation of the current MCAM system for certain applications, with citation.

claim: A number of strategies are available to increase MCAM sampling rates, including utilizing an updated version of USB that allows approximately 10X faster data transfer.
source: The most straightforward paths to directly increasing the MCAM frame rate are (1) utilizing an updated version of USB that now allows approximately 10 X faster data transfer, (2) distributing data transmission across multiple desktop computers, (3) adopting an alternative FPGA data transfer scheme (e.g. replacing USB data transmission with a faster PCIe protocol), and (4) executing on-chip pixel binning, image cropping, and/or lossless compression to increase temporal sampling rates at the expense of spatial sampling.
evidence: This describes potential future improvements to the MCAM system.

claim: Various combinations of strategies to increase frame rate are currently being explored to facilitate true video-rate (24–30 Hz) MCAM imaging and to achieve significantly higher frame rates and improve cross-camera snapshot synchronization.
source: Various combinations of the above strategies are currently being explored to facilitate true video-rate (24–30 Hz) MCAM imaging and to achieve significantly higher frame rates and improve cross-camera snapshot synchronization.
evidence: This describes ongoing development efforts to improve the MCAM system.

claim: A promising direction is to dynamically pre-process acquired images on the included FPGAs before directing them to computer memory to lighten data transfer loads.
source: A third promising direction is to dynamically pre-process acquired images on the included FPGAs before directing them to computer memory to lighten data transfer loads.
evidence: This describes a potential future improvement to the MCAM system.

claim: CMOS sensors with increased sensitivity and a higher imaging NA could increase fluorescence signal-to-noise ratio and potentially facilitate fluorescence detection at the cellular scale.
source: Second, while we have demonstrated the MCAM's fundamental ability to acquire wide-field fluorescence video of dynamic organism movement (see Supplement), CMOS sensors with increased sensitivity and a higher imaging NA could increase fluorescence signal-to-noise ratio and potentially facilitate fluorescence detect at the cellular scale.
evidence: This describes a potential future improvement to the MCAM's fluorescence imaging capabilities.

claim: Improvements in ratiometric acquisition and the potential addition of optical sectioning could increase fluorescence signal fidelity, most notably during rapid organism movement.
source: Improvements in ratiometric acquisition and the potential addition of optical sectioning could also increase fluorescence signal fidelity, most notably during rapid organism movement.
evidence: This describes potential future improvements to the MCAM's fluorescence imaging capabilities.

claim: With appropriate effort, the MCAM architecture could soon unlock high-quality measurement of functional fluorescence activity during free organism movement over truly macroscopic areas.
source: With appropriate effort, the MCAM architecture could soon unlock high-quality measurement of functional fluorescence activity during free organism movement over truly macroscopic areas, thus yielding a new imaging platform for neuroscientific experiment.
evidence: This is a speculative claim about the future potential of the MCAM for neuroscience applications.

claim: The demonstrated lateral resolution of 18 µm full-pitch is typically not sufficient to resolve individual cells unless they are sparsely labeled.
source: Finally, while the demonstrated lateral resolution in this work (18 µm full-pitch) is typically not sufficient to resolve individual cells unless they are sparsely labeled, tighter camera packing and updated imaging optics may unlock the ability to observe cellular-scale detail in future designs.
evidence: This is a stated limitation of the current MCAM system's resolution.

claim: Tighter camera packing and updated imaging optics may unlock the ability to observe cellular-scale detail in future MCAM designs.
source: Finally, while the demonstrated lateral resolution in this work (18 µm full-pitch) is typically not sufficient to resolve individual cells unless they are sparsely labeled, tighter camera packing and updated imaging optics may unlock the ability to observe cellular-scale detail in future designs.
evidence: This describes a potential future improvement to the MCAM's resolution capabilities.

claim: Large area, high-resolution imaging is important in industrial inspection of manufactured goods and materials, as well as semiconductor metrology.
source: Large area, high-resolution imaging is important in industrial inspection of manufactured goods (Yang et al., 2020) and materials (Ngan et al., 2011), as well as semiconductor metrology (Huang and Pan, 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published research on industrial imaging applications.

claim: Large area, high-resolution imaging methods are required for defect detection on semiconductor wafer surfaces.
source: For instance, such methods are required for defect detection on semiconductor wafer surfaces.
evidence: This is an example of an industrial application for large area, high-resolution imaging.

claim: Large area, high-resolution imaging can unlock new functionalities in imaging large pathology specimens, such as whole-mount brain slices.
source: It can also unlock new functionalities in imaging large pathology specimens, such as whole-mount brain slices (Axer et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to published research on pathology imaging, suggesting a potential application for the MCAM.

claim: Biological researchers may be able to utilize the MCAM platform to monitor bacterial colonies and cell cultures over macroscopically large areas.
source: Biological researchers may also be able to utilize the MCAM platform to monitor bacterial colonies (Shi et al., 2017) and cell cultures over macroscopically large areas.
evidence: This is a speculative claim about potential biological applications of the MCAM, with citation.

claim: The MCAM architecture fits within a growing body of computational imaging hardware that is specifically designed not for direct human viewing, but with the assumption that data post-processing will be used to extract relevant information.
source: In summary, our MCAM architecture fits within a growing body of computational imaging hardware (Mait et al., 2018) that is specifically designed not for direct human viewing, but instead with the assumption that data post-processing will be used to extract relevant information for subsequent analysis.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to published research on computational imaging, placing the MCAM in context.

claim: Simultaneously improving processing software (e.g. 3D organism tracking, machine learning-assisted analysis) will prove critical to fully realize the MCAM's benefits.
source: While novel display technology currently enables visual assessment of the MCAM's gigapixel videos that can be many Terabytes in raw size, we anticipate that simultaneously improving processing software (e.g. 3D organism tracking, machine learning-assisted analysis) will prove critical to fully realize the microscope's benefits.
evidence: This is a claim about the importance of software development for the MCAM.

claim: As image sensor technology continues to improve with automated processing moving on-chip, the parallelized imaging architecture can help overcome the standard tradeoff between resolution and field-of-view while yielding manageable information-rich datasets.
source: As image sensor technology continues to improve with such automated processing moving on-chip (Amir et al., 2018; Posch et al., 2014), we anticipate that our parallelized imaging architecture can help overcome the standard tradeoff between resolution and field-of-view while at the same time yield manageable information-rich datasets to provide new insight into complex biological systems.
evidence: This is a forward-looking claim about the future potential of the MCAM architecture, with citations to on-chip processing technology.

claim: A Faster-RCNN object detection network was adapted to automate the detection of zebrafish in stitched MCAM images.
source: We adapted a convolutional neural network (CNN)-based object detection algorithm (Faster-RCNN) to automate the detection of zebrafish in stitched MCAM images (Figure 2A), which are too large for training or inference on existing graphical processing units (GPUs).
evidence: This describes the use of a CNN for object detection in MCAM images, shown in Figure 2A.

claim: MCAM images are too large for training or inference on existing graphical processing units (GPUs).
source: We adapted a convolutional neural network (CNN)-based object detection algorithm (Faster-RCNN) to automate the detection of zebrafish in stitched MCAM images (Figure 2A), which are too large for training or inference on existing graphical processing units (GPUs).
evidence: This is a stated technical challenge of working with gigapixel MCAM images.

claim: Transfer learning with a data augmentation pipeline that included supplementing training data with synthetically generated occluder fish yielded a network that could accurately detect individual zebrafish even when they occluded one another.
source: We used transfer learning with a data augmentation pipeline that included supplementing training data with synthetically generated occluder fish (similar to that described in István et al., 2018; Sárándi et al., 2018), because occlusion was relatively rare in the original data. After training, this yielded a network that could accurately detect individual zebrafish even when they occluded one another (Appendix 1—figure 5I, Video 3).
evidence: This describes the training approach and results for the zebrafish detection network, with results shown in Appendix 1—figure 5I and Video 3.

claim: The high spatial resolution of the MCAM was exploited to consistently recognize individual zebrafish by morphological differences.
source: To track individual zebrafish over time, we exploited the high spatial resolution of the MCAM to consistently recognize individuals by morphological differences (Figure 2B), which has not been shown before in zebrafish younger than 21 days old.
evidence: This describes a novel capability enabled by the MCAM's resolution, shown in Figure 2B.

claim: Consistent recognition of individual zebrafish by morphological differences has not been shown before in zebrafish younger than 21 days old.
source: To track individual zebrafish over time, we exploited the high spatial resolution of the MCAM to consistently recognize individuals by morphological differences (Figure 2B), which has not been shown before in zebrafish younger than 21 days old.
evidence: This is a claim about the novelty of the zebrafish identification capability.

claim: A Siamese neural network was trained that was able to learn to track the same zebrafish across multiple frames.
source: Specifically, we trained a Siamese neural network (Bertinetto et al., 2021; Appendix 1—figure 6) that was able to learn to track the same zebrafish across multiple frames (Figure 2C).
evidence: This describes the use of a Siamese neural network for zebrafish tracking, with results shown in Figure 2C.

claim: The Siamese neural network had unique access to idiosyncrasies in melanophore patterns, structural and overall body morphology when learning to distinguish individual animals.
source: Given the high spatial resolution of the MCAM, this network had unique access to idiosyncrasies in melanophore patterns, structural and overall body morphology when learning to distinguish individual animals.
evidence: This explains how the MCAM's resolution enabled the neural network to distinguish individual zebrafish.

claim: The MCAM's resolution was used to identify behavioral details of each zebrafish by performing tail tracking and eye position measurement.
source: In addition, we used the MCAM's resolution to identify behavioral details of each zebrafish by performing tail tracking (Figure 2D) and eye position measurement (Figure 2E), which yielded aggregate statistics over populations of zebrafish during free swimming.
evidence: This describes behavioral analysis capabilities enabled by the MCAM's resolution, shown in Figures 2D and 2E.

claim: The MCAM's multi-lens architecture offers novel measurement capabilities as compared to standard single-lens microscopes.
source: In addition, the MCAM's multi-lens architecture offers novel measurement capabilities as compared to standard single-lens microscopes.
evidence: This is a general claim about the advantages of the MCAM's architecture.

claim: By using rectangular image sensors, the MCAM provides images from adjacent cameras that overlap approximately 50% in the x-direction and <10% in the y-direction to facilitate stitching.
source: By using rectangular image sensors (16:9 aspect ratio), the MCAM provides images from adjacent cameras that overlap approximately 50% in the x-direction and <10% in the y-direction to facilitate stitching (Appendix 1—figure 2).
evidence: This describes the overlapping field-of-view configuration, shown in Appendix 1—figure 2.

claim: The overlapping field-of-view configuration ensures that any point in the sample plane is simultaneously observed by at least two cameras.
source: This overlap ensures that any point in the sample plane is simultaneously observed by at least two cameras and allows us to use positional disparities from matched features (i.e. stereoscopic depth measurement techniques) to calculate the depth of objects within adjacent camera image pairs (Figure 2F, Methods).
evidence: This explains how the overlapping configuration enables stereoscopic depth measurement, shown in Figure 2F.

claim: After matching features within adjacent frames using a scale-invariant feature transform, pixel-level lateral feature displacements generate depth estimates using known MCAM imaging system parameters.
source: Briefly, after matching features within adjacent frames using a scale-invariant feature transform, pixel-level lateral feature displacements generate depth estimates using known MCAM imaging system parameters (e.g. inter-camera spacing and working distance).
evidence: This describes the stereoscopic depth measurement algorithm used with the MCAM.

claim: Example 3D tracking revealed typical quantifiable signatures of fish spontaneous swim trajectories along spatial axes typically inaccessible without dual view camera systems.
source: Example 3D tracking revealed typical quantifiable signatures of fish spontaneous swim trajectories along spatial axes typically inaccessible (Bolton et al., 2019) without dual view camera systems.
evidence: This is a claim about the novel capabilities of the MCAM's 3D tracking, with citation to prior work.

claim: The MCAM is a general, scalable imaging platform that can be used in the study of multiple model organisms.
source: The MCAM is a general, scalable imaging platform that can be used in the study of multiple model organisms.
evidence: This is a general claim about the versatility of the MCAM, supported by demonstrations with multiple species.

claim: A CNN-based segmentation algorithm was employed to detect C. elegans in MCAM images.
source: We plated these worms on a large, square (24.5cmx24.5cm) petri dish and employed a CNN-based segmentation algorithm (Appendix 1) Videos captured ~58,000 worms per frame, captured at about 450 pixels per worm within a typical gigapixel video (averaged across 20 frames, single frame in Figure 3A–C, top).
evidence: This describes the use of a CNN for C. elegans detection in MCAM images.

claim: Computer vision algorithms were used to track worms and detect swarm formation.
source: Using computer vision algorithms to track worms and detect swarm formation shows how such large-scale differences in behavior can be observed with the MCAM (Video 4, Video 5 and Video 6).
evidence: This describes the use of computer vision for analyzing C. elegans behavior, shown in Videos 4-6.
